title: Not ten thousand years
hook: don't act as if you'll live ten thousand years; while you can, be good (Meditations 4.17)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus on taking away the opinion. Your line was take away the label. When something stung, could you split the event from the label? Day five hundred fifty-four.

Ten thousand years. That's the number Marcus Aurelius chose, and it's meant to be absurd. Nobody plans on living that long. And yet a thank-you waits a season, then a year. An apology stays ready in the head and never reaches the mouth. A visit to an aunt who keeps saying come anytime slides to some later month, as though later were endless. In the seventeenth entry of book four, Marcus wrote himself a reminder short enough to fit on a sticky note. Today: not ten thousand years.
screen: `TEN THOUSAND YEARS.` → `AS THOUGH LATER WERE ENDLESS.` → `NOT TEN THOUSAND YEARS.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In George Long's 1862 translation it reads: "Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good." Three sentences. A warning, a fact, and an instruction. Second, ten thousand years. That number is the joke inside the warning. Marcus isn't accusing himself of a belief. He's accusing himself of a habit: putting off the good because there always seems to be more time. Third, death hangs over you. Marcus doesn't say this to frighten himself. Stoic writers kept death in view on purpose, as a way of sorting what matters from what doesn't. If this might be the last week, the thank-you note moves up, and the argument about the thermostat moves down. Fourth, while you can, be good. Notice he doesn't say be productive, or be famous, or finish your list. He says be good. And he puts a condition on it: while it is in your power. Not when you're less busy. Not when the kids are grown. Not when you've earned a rest. The good you've been saving isn't kept somewhere safe. It's quietly expiring. Here's the Tuesday version. Think of one good act you've been holding for later. Then ask: is later actually promised? Marcus's answer, in three short sentences, was no.
screen: `A WARNING, A FACT, AN INSTRUCTION.` · `NOT A BELIEF, A HABIT.` · `DEATH IN VIEW, TO SORT WHAT MATTERS.` · `WHILE IT IS IN YOUR POWER.` · then, large: `BE GOOD WHILE I CAN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the number ten thousand sit there for a moment, and smile at it if you like. Then come back to this one hour. Who will you see in it? A coworker, a child, a stranger at the counter, a voice on the phone. Choose one. Ask quietly: what would being good to them look like, in the next hour? Something small: a real thank-you, full attention, a patient answer. Picture doing it. The bell holds the time.
George Long, whose 1862 translation renders Marcus's warning: do not act as if you had ten thousand years, but be good while it's in your power. Today's word.
Your line: be good while I can. Do one good thing today for whoever is in front of you, without waiting for a better moment. Day five hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius use Meditations 4.17 as a prompt to stop postponing small kindnesses.

fork.reveal: Marcus says don't act as if you had ten thousand years: while it is in your power, be good.

original.note: Greek, 'good': Marcus's instruction in 4.17 is simply to become good while you can.

trapdoor: what you thought: life is short, so enjoy it.
what it means: life is short, so do the good you've been saving, now.
what a scholar hears: keeping death in view, later called memento mori, was a Stoic discipline for sorting priorities, not for gloom.
recall: blood, bones, a net of nerves

notes: Quoted from George Long's 1862 translation, 4.17, from memory: please verify word for word against the 1862 text. If it differs, convert to paraphrase.
Marcus and Faustina lost a number of their children young; 'lost several of his own children' should be confirmed (the Historia Augusta and other sources).
'Memento mori' is a later Latin phrase, not Marcus's own; the trapdoor says 'later called'. Confirm wording.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced 'an emperor who had lost several of his own children' (the earlier note on it is now moot); hook rebuilt around the number so it no longer tells the listener what they have been putting off; practice and carry refocused on being good in the next hour, because the 'pick one postponed thing and decide when' practice repeated days 540 and 548; 'the Stoics' to 'Stoic writers'; 'often' to 'some'.
